classification.difficultyReason: Use the hinted intercept form and limiting point to determine the quadratic's scale, then use symmetry to calculate and interpret its maximum height.

content.prompt:
A professional tennis player returns a ball from ground level. It was hit in such a way that it will cover a horizontal distance of 22 m and land just inside the opposite end of the court.

The opponent is standing 4 m from the baseline and he can hit any ball less than 3 m high.

What is the lowest maximum height the ball must reach to fly over the opponent and win the point?

(Hint: Find the equation of the parabola using the $x$-intercepts and the point $(4,3)$.)

spec.description: Unshaded contextual schematic retaining the ball markers, right-to-left travel arrows, opponent, tennis net and all three measurements. The opponent is represented by an editable simple figure.
spec.mathematics: Ground endpoints are 22 m apart. The limiting path passes through a point 4 m from the left endpoint at height 3 m. The curve is equation-derived; no equation or calculated maximum is printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent supplied contextual diagram; calculated model and maximum remain answer-only.

answer.short: $\frac{121}{24}\text{ m}=5\frac{1}{24}\text{ m}$. Use the intercepts to obtain $h=-\frac{1}{24}x(x-22)$; its maximum occurs at $x=11$.
answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the height in metres and $x$ the distance in metres from the left endpoint. The intercepts are $x=0$ and $x=22$.

$$\begin{align*}h&=kx(x-22)\\3&=k(4)(4-22)\\3&=-72k\\k&=-\frac{1}{24}\\h&=-\frac{1}{24}x(x-22)\end{align*}$$

The turning point lies midway between the intercepts.

$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{0+22}{2}\\x&=11\\h&=-\frac{1}{24}(11)(11-22)\\h&=\frac{121}{24}\end{align*}$$

The parabola is concave down, so the lowest maximum height is $5\dfrac{1}{24}\text{ m}$. At this limiting height, the ball is 3 m high at the opponent.
